mn26:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.
mn26:2.1: Then when it was morning, the Blessed One dressed, and taking his bowl and (outer) robe, he went into Sāvatthī for alms.
mn26:2.2: Then many bhikkhus went to the venerable Ānanda and said to him:
mn26:2.3: ‘Friend Ānanda, it is long since we heard a talk on the Dhamma from the Blessed One’s own lips.
mn26:2.4: It would be good if we could do so, friend Ānanda.’
mn26:2.5: ‘Then let the venerable ones go to Rammaka the divine’s retreat;
mn26:2.6: perhaps you will hear a talk on the Dhamma from the Blessed One’s own lips.’
mn26:3.1: Now when the Blessed One had wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and had returned from his alms-round after his meal, he addressed the venerable Ānanda:
mn26:3.2: ‘Ānanda let us go to the Eastern Park, to the Palace of Migāra’s mother, for the day’s abiding.’
mn26:3.3: ‘Even so, venerable sir,’ the venerable Ānanda replied.
mn26:3.4: Then the Blessed One went with the venerable Ānanda to the Eastern Park, the Palace of Migāra’s mother, for the day’s abiding.
mn26:3.5: Now when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from meditation, and he addressed the venerable Ānanda:
mn26:3.6: ‘Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern bathing place and bathe our limbs.’
mn26:3.7: ‘Even so, venerable sir,’ the venerable Ānanda replied.
mn26:3.8: Then the Blessed One went with the venerable Ānanda to the Eastern bathing place to bathe his limbs.
mn26:3.9: When he had done so, he came up out of the water and stood in one robe drying his limbs.
mn26:3.11: ‘Venerable sir, Rammaka the divine’s retreat is nearby.
mn26:3.14: Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One went there out of pity.’
mn26:3.15: The Blessed One consented in silence.
mn26:4.1: Then the Blessed One went to Rammaka the divine’s retreat.
mn26:4.2: Now on that occasion many bhikkhus had gathered together there to discuss the Dhamma.
mn26:4.3: The Blessed One stood outside the door waiting for the end of their discussion.
mn26:4.4: When he knew that it was finished, he coughed and knocked.
mn26:4.5: The bhikkhus opened the door for him.
mn26:4.6: Then he went inside and sat down on a seat made ready.
mn26:4.7: When he had done so he addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn26:4.8: ‘Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now? And what was your discussion meanwhile, which was left unfinished?’
mn26:4.9: ‘Venerable sir, our discussion which was left unfinished was about the Dhamma and it was about the Blessed One himself. Then the Blessed One arrived.’
mn26:4.11: It becomes you that as clansmen who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, you gather for discussion of the Dhamma.
mn26:4.12: When you are gathered together there are two alternatives:
mn26:4.13: discussion of the Dhamma or the Noble Ones’ silence.
mn26:5.1: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of search:
mn26:5.2: the noble search and the ignoble search.
mn26:5.3: And what is the ignoble search?
mn26:5.4: Here someone, himself subject to the birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement, seeks what is also subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement.
mn26:6.1: ‘And what may be said to be subject to birth?
mn26:6.2: Wife and children are subject to birth, and so are bondswomen and bondsmen, goats and sheep, fowls and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses and mares, gold and silver.
mn26:6.3: These essentials of existence are subject to birth;
mn26:6.4: and one who is entangled with these and unwarily committed to them is one who, being himself subject to birth, seeks what is also subject to birth.
mn26:7.1: ‘And what may be said to be subject to ageing?
mn26:7.2: Wife and children are subject to ageing and so are … gold and silver.
mn26:7.3: These essentials of existence are subject to ageing;
mn26:7.4: and one who is entangled with these and unwarily committed to them is one who, being himself subject to ageing, seeks what is also subject to ageing.
mn26:8.1: ‘And what may be said to be subject to ailment?
mn26:8.2: Wife and children are subject to ailment and so are … gold and silver.
mn26:8.3: These essentials of existence are subject to ailment …
mn26:8.4: seeks what is also subject to ailment.
mn26:9.1: ‘And what may be said to be subject to death?
mn26:9.2: Wife and children are subject to death and so are … gold and silver
mn26:9.3: These essentials of existence are subject to death …
mn26:9.4: seeks what is also subject to death.
mn26:10.1: ‘And what may be said to be subject to sorrow?
mn26:10.2: Wife and children are subject to sorrow and so are … gold and silver.
mn26:10.3: These essentials of existence are subject to sorrow …
mn26:10.4: seeks what is also subject to sorrow.
mn26:11.1: ‘And what may be said to be subject to defilement?
mn26:11.2: Wife and children are subject to defilement and so are bondswomen and bondsmen, goats and sheep, fowls and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses and mares, gold and silver.
mn26:11.3: These essentials of existence are subject to defilement,
mn26:11.4: and one who is entangled with these and unwarily committed to them is one who being himself subject to defilement, seeks what is also subject to defilement.
mn26:12.2: Here someone, himself subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement, and knowing the danger in these dhammas, seeks the unborn, unageing, unailing, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled, supreme surcease of bondage, which is Nibbāna.
mn26:13.1: ‘Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta, I too, being myself subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement, sought what was also subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement.
mn26:13.3: “Why, being myself subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement, do I seek what is also subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement?
mn26:13.4: Suppose that, myself being subject to these dhammas, knowing the danger in these dhammas, I seek the unborn, unageing, unailing, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled, supreme surcease of bondage, which is Nibbāna?”’
mn26:14.1: ‘Later, while still a boy, a black-haired youth endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first phase of life, I shaved off my hair and beard—though my mother and father wished otherwise and grieved with tearful faces—I put on the yellow cloth and went forth from the house life into homelessness.
mn26:15.1: ‘Having gone forth in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and I said to him:
mn26:15.2: “Friend Kālāma, I want to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and Discipline.”’
mn26:15.3: ‘When this was said, Āḷāra Kālāma replied:
mn26:15.5: This Dhamma is such that in no long time a wise man can enter upon and abide in it, himself realizing through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.”
mn26:15.7: I claimed that as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teachings went I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and that I knew and saw—and there were others that did likewise.
mn26:15.9: “It is not through mere faith alone the Āḷāra Kālāma declares his Dhamma; (he does so) because he enters upon and abides in it, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:15.10: Certainly Āḷāra Kālāma abides in this Dhamma knowing and seeing.”’
mn26:15.11: ‘Then I went to Ālāra Kālāma, and I said to him:
mn26:15.12: “Friend Kālāma, in what way do you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?”’
mn26:15.13: ‘When this was said, he declared the base consisting of nothingness.
mn26:15.15: “Not only Ālāra Kālāma has faith; I too have faith.
mn26:15.16: Not only Ālāra Kālāma has energy; I too have energy.
mn26:15.17: Not only Ālāra Kālāma has mindfulness; I too have mindfulness.
mn26:15.18: Not only Ālāra Kālāma has concentration; I too have concentration.
mn26:15.19: Not only Ālāra Kālāma has understanding; I too have understanding.
mn26:15.20: Suppose I exercise control in order to realize the Dhamma that he declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge?”’
mn26:15.21: ‘I soon entered upon and abode in that Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:15.22: Then I went to Ālāra Kālāma, and I said to him:
mn26:15.23: “Friend Kālāma, is it in this way that you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?”’
mn26:15.24: ”It is in this way, friend, that I declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.”’
mn26:15.25: ”Friend, I too in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.”’
mn26:15.26: ”It is gain for us, friend, it is great gain for us
mn26:15.27: that we have such a venerable one as our companion in the life divine.
mn26:15.28: So the Dhamma that I declare to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:15.29: And the Dhamma that you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma I declare to have entered upon, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:15.30: So you know the Dhamma that I know; I know the Dhamma that you know.
mn26:15.31: As I am, so you are; as you are, so am I.
mn26:15.32: Come, friend, let us now lead this community together.”’
mn26:15.33: ‘Thus Ālāra Kālāma, my Teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equal footing with himself, and awarded me the highest honour.’
mn26:15.35: “This Dhamma does not lead to dispassion, to fading of lust, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna, but only to the base consisting of nothingness.”’
mn26:15.36: ‘I was not satisfied with that Dhamma. I left it and went away.
mn26:16.1: ‘Still in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta, and I said to him:
mn26:16.2: “Friend, I went to lead the life divine in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
mn26:16.3: ‘When this was said, Uddaka Rāmaputta replied:
mn26:16.5: This Dhamma is such that in no long time a wise man can enter upon and abide in it, himself realizing through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine.”
mn26:16.7: I claimed that as far as mere lip-reciting and rehearsal of his teaching went I could speak with knowledge and assurance, and that I knew and saw—and there were others who did likewise.
mn26:16.9: “It is not through mere faith alone that Rāma declares his Dhamma, but (he does so) because he enters upon and abides in it, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:16.10: Certainly Rāma abides in this Dhamma knowing and seeing.”
mn26:16.11: ‘Then I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta, and I said to him:
mn26:16.12: “Friend Rāma, in what way do you declare to have entered upon this Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?”
mn26:16.13: ‘When this was said, he declared the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn26:16.15: “Not only Rāma has faith; I too have faith.
mn26:16.16: Not only Rāma has energy; I too have energy.
mn26:16.17: Not only Rāma has mindfulness; I too have mindfulness.
mn26:16.18: Not only Rāma has concentration; I too have concentration.
mn26:16.19: Not only Rāma has understanding; I too have understanding.
mn26:16.20: Suppose I exercise control in order to realize the Dhamma that he declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge?”
mn26:16.21: ‘I soon entered upon and abode in that Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:16.22: Then I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and I said to him:
mn26:16.23: “Friend Rāma, is it in this way that you declare to have entered upon the Dhamma, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge?”
mn26:16.24: ”It is in this way, friend, that Rāma declares to have entered upon the Dhamma, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.”
mn26:16.25: “Friend, I too in this way enter upon and abide in this Dhamma, myself realizing it through direct knowledge.”
mn26:16.26: ”It is gain for us, friend, it is great gain for us,
mn26:16.27: that we have such a venerable one for our companion in the life divine.
mn26:16.28: So the Dhamma that Rāma declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:16.29: And the Dhamma that you enter upon and abide in, yourself realizing it through direct knowledge, that Dhamma Rāma declares to have entered upon, himself realizing it through direct knowledge.
mn26:16.30: So you know that Dhamma that Rāma knows; Rāma knows the Dhamma that you know.
mn26:16.31: As Rāma is, so you are; as you are, so Rāma is.
mn26:16.32: Come, friend, do you now lead this community.”
mn26:16.33: ‘Thus Uddaka Rāmaputta, my companion in the life divine, placed me in the Teacher’s place and accorded me the highest honour.
mn26:16.35: “This Dhamma does not lead to dispassion, to fading of lust, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna; but only to the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
mn26:16.36: ‘I was not satisfied with that Dhamma. I left it and went away.
mn26:17.1: ‘Still in search of what is profitable, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country, till at length I arrived at Senānigama near Uruvelā.
mn26:17.2: There I saw an agreeable piece of ground, a delightful grove, a clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village as alms resort.
mn26:17.4: “There is this agreeable piece of ground, this delightful grove, this clear-flowing river with pleasant smooth banks, and nearby a village for alms resort.
mn26:17.5: This will serve for the endeavour of a clansman who seeks endeavour.”
mn26:18.1: ‘Being myself subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement, knowing the danger in these dhammas, seeking the unborn, unageing, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled supreme surcease of bondage, which is Nibbāna, I attained the unborn, unageing, unailing, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled supreme surcease of bondage, which is Nibbāna.
mn26:18.2: ‘The knowledge and vision arose in me:
mn26:18.3: “My deliverance is unassailable. This my last birth. There is now no renewal of being.”’
mn26:19.2: “This Dhamma that I have attained is profound, hard to see and hard to discover. It is (the most) peaceful and superior (goal of all), unattainable by (mere) ratiocination, subtle, and for the wise to experience.
mn26:19.3: But this generation loves something to rely on, delights in something to rely on, is glad of something to rely on.
mn26:19.4: It is hard for such a generation to see this truth, namely, specific conditionality, dependent origination.
mn26:19.5: And it is hard to see this truth, namely, the stilling of all formations, relinquishing of all essentials of existence, exhaustion of craving, fading of lust, cessation, Nibbāna.
mn26:19.6: And if I taught the Dhamma, others would not understand me, and that would be weariness and a bother for me.”
mn26:19.7: ‘In fact, there came to me spontaneously these stanzas never heard before:
mn26:19.9: That even I found hard to reach;
mn26:19.10: For it will never be perceived
mn26:19.11: By those who live in lust and hate.
mn26:19.12: Men dyed in lust, and whom a cloud
mn26:19.13: Of darkness laps, will never see
mn26:19.14: What goes against the stream, is subtle,
mn26:19.15: Deep, and hard to see, abstruse.
mn26:19.16: ‘Considering thus, my mind favoured inaction instead of teaching the Dhamma.
mn26:20.1: ‘Then the (Brahmā) Divinity Sahampati knew in mind the thought in my mind, and he (considered):
mn26:20.2: “The world will be lost, the world will be utterly lost, since the mind of the Tathāgata, Arahant and Fully Enlightened One, favours inaction instead of teaching the Dhamma.”
mn26:20.3: ‘Then just as soon as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, the Divinity Sahampati vanished in the world of the Divinity and appeared before me.
mn26:20.4: Then he arranged his upper robe on one shoulder and raising his hands palms together towards me, he said:
mn26:20.5: “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma.
mn26:20.6: There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are wasting through not hearing the Dhamma.
mn26:20.7: Some of them will gain final knowledge of the Dhamma.”
mn26:20.9: and having done so, he said further:
mn26:20.10: In Magadha till now have Dhammas been
mn26:20.11: Unpurified, thought out by those still stained.
mn26:20.12: Open the Deathless gateway, let them hear
mn26:20.13: The Dhamma the Immaculate has found;
mn26:20.14: Who stands upon a solid pile of rock,
mn26:20.15: And, just as one sees all the folk around,
mn26:20.18: This human breed engulfed in sorrowing
mn26:20.19: That Birth has at its mercy, and Old Age.
mn26:20.21: Free from all debt, and wander in the world.
mn26:20.22: Proclaim the Dhamma; there are some,
mn26:21.1: ‘Then I listened to the Divinity’s pleading. Out of compassion for beings I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.
mn26:21.2: Surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some that dwelt seeing fear in blame and in the other world.
mn26:21.3: Just as in a pond of blue or red or white lotuses, some lotuses that are born and grow in the water thrive immersed in the water without rising out of it, and some other lotuses that are born and grow in water rest on the water’s surface, and some other lotuses that are born and grow in the water rise out of the water and stand clear, unwetted by it,
mn26:21.4: so too, surveying the world … and some that dwelt seeing fear in blame and in the other world.
mn26:21.5: ‘Then I replied to the Divinity Sahampati in stanzas:
mn26:21.6: Open for them are the Deathless’ doors,
mn26:21.7: Let those that hear now show their faith,
mn26:21.8: Seeing the bother I spoke not for men
mn26:21.10: ‘Then the Divinity Sahampati (thought): “I have made it possible for the Dhamma to be taught by the Blessed One.” And after paying homage to me, keeping me on the right, the Divinity departed.
mn26:22.2: “To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
mn26:22.3: Who will soon understand this Dhamma?”
mn26:22.5: “Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, learned and discerning. He has long had little dust in his eyes.
mn26:22.6: Suppose I taught the Dhamma first to Āḷāra Kālāma?
mn26:22.9: “Venerable sir, Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago.”
mn26:22.10: And the knowledge and vision arose in me:
mn26:22.13: “Āḷāra Kālāma’s loss is a great one.
mn26:22.14: If he had heard this Dhamma, he would soon have understood it.”
mn26:23.2: “To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
mn26:23.3: Who will soon understand this Dhamma?”
mn26:23.5: “Uddaka Rāmaputta is wise, learned and discerning. He has long had little dust in his eyes.
mn26:23.6: Suppose I taught the Dhamma first to Uddaka Rāmaputta?
mn26:23.9: “Venerable sir, Uddaka Rāmaputta died last night.”
mn26:23.10: And the knowledge and vision in me:
mn26:23.13: “Uddaka Rāmaputta’s loss is a great one.
mn26:23.14: If he had heard this Dhamma, he would soon have understood it.”
mn26:24.2: “To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
mn26:24.3: Who will soon understand this Dhamma?”
mn26:24.5: “The bhikkhus of the group of five, who attended me while I was engaged in the struggle for control were very helpful.
mn26:24.6: Suppose I taught the Dhamma first to them?”’
mn26:24.8: “Where are the bhikkhus of the group of five living now?”
mn26:24.9: And with the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw that they were living at Benares in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
mn26:24.10: ‘Then when I had stayed at Uruvela as long as I chose, I set out to go by stages to Benares.
mn26:25.1: Between Gayā and the Place of Enlightenment the monk Upaka saw me on the road.
mn26:25.3: “Friend, the colour of your skin is pure and bright.
mn26:25.4: Under whom have you gone forth, friend? Or who is your Teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you confess?”
mn26:25.5: ‘When this was said, I replied to the monk Upaka in stanzas:
mn26:25.6: Transcender of all being, All-knower am I,
mn26:25.7: Unsullied in all dhammas, renouncing them all
mn26:25.8: By craving’s ceasing freed. And this do I owe
mn26:25.9: To my own wit, to whom should I concede it?
mn26:25.10: I have no Teacher, and my like
mn26:25.11: Exists nowhere in all the world
mn26:25.12: With all its gods, because I have
mn26:25.14: I am the Teacher in the world
mn26:25.15: Without a peer, an Arahant too
mn26:25.16: And I alone am Full enlightened
mn26:25.17: Quenched, whose fires are quite extinct.
mn26:25.18: I go to Kāsi’s city now
mn26:25.19: To set in motion the Dhamma’s Wheel:
mn26:25.21: I go to beat the Deathless Drum.
mn26:25.22: ‘“By your claims, friend, you ought to be a Victor Universal.”
mn26:25.24: Are these won to exhaustion of taints.
mn26:25.26: For that I am a Victor.
mn26:25.27: ‘When this was said, the monk Upaka said: “May it be so, friend.” Shaking his head, he took a by-path and departed.
mn26:26.1: ‘Then wandering by stages, I came at length to Benares, to the Deer Park at Isipatana, where the bhikkhus of the group of five were.
mn26:26.2: ‘They saw me coming at a distance,
mn26:26.3: and they agreed among themselves thus:
mn26:26.4: “Friends, here comes the monk Gotama who turned self-indulgent, shirked control and reverted to luxury.
mn26:26.5: We ought not to pay homage to him or rise up for him or receive his bowl and robe.
mn26:26.6: But a seat can be prepared for him. If he likes, he will sit down.”
mn26:26.7: ‘However, as soon as I approached, they found themselves unable to keep their pact.
mn26:26.8: One came to meet me and took my bowl and (outer) robe; another prepared a seat; and another got water ready for my feet;
mn26:26.9: and they addressed me by name as “friend”.
mn26:27.1: ‘When this was said, I told them:
mn26:27.2: “Bhikkhus, do not address a Tathāgata by name as ‘friend’.
mn26:27.3: A Tathāgata is an Arahant and Fully Enlightened.
mn26:27.4: Listen, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I shall instruct you; I shall teach you the Dhamma.
mn26:27.5: By practising as you are instructed, you will, by realization yourselves here and now through direct knowledge enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the life divine on account of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
mn26:27.6: ‘When this was said, the bhikkhus of the group of five answered me thus:
mn26:27.7: “Friend Gotama, with the behaviour the way, and the difficult feats, which you practised you achieved no distinction worthy of a Noble One’s knowledge and vision higher than the human state (dhamma). Since you have now turned self-indulgent, shirked control and reverted to luxury, how will you have achieved any such distinction?”
mn26:27.8: ‘When this was said, I told them:
mn26:27.9: “A Tathāgata is not one who has turned self-indulgent, nor has he shirked control and reverted to luxury.
mn26:27.10: A Tathāgata is an Arahant and Fully Enlightened.
mn26:27.11: Listen, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I shall instruct you; I shall teach you the Dhamma.
mn26:27.12: By practising as you are instructed, you will, by realization yourselves here and now through direct knowledge enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the life divine on account of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
mn26:27.13: ‘A second time the bhikkhus of the group of five said to me:
mn26:27.14: “Friend Gotama … how will you have achieved any such distinction?”
mn26:27.16: “A Tathāgata is not one who has turned self-indulgent …
mn26:27.17: from the home life into homelessness.”
mn26:27.18: ‘A third time the bhikkhus of the group of five said to me:
mn26:27.19: “Friend Gotama … how will you have achieved any such distinction?”
mn26:28.1: ‘When this was said I asked them:
mn26:28.2: “Bhikkhus, have you ever known me to speak like this before?”’
mn26:28.4: “Bhikkhus, a Tathāgata is an Arahant and Fully Enlightened.
mn26:28.5: Listen, bhikkhus, the Deathless has been attained. I shall instruct you; I shall teach you the Dhamma.
mn26:28.6: By practising as you are instructed, you will, by realization yourselves here and now through direct knowledge enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the life divine on account of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.”’
mn26:29.1: ‘I was able to convince the bhikkhus of the group of five.
mn26:29.2: Sometimes I instructed two bhikkhus while three went for alms;
mn26:29.3: and we six lived upon what the three brought back from their alms-round.
mn26:29.4: Sometimes I instructed three bhikkhus while two went for alms:
mn26:29.5: and we six lived upon what the two brought back from their alms-round.
mn26:30.1: ‘Then the bhikkhus of the group of five, thus taught and instructed by me, being themselves subject to birth, ageing, ailment, death, sorrow and defilement, knowing the danger in these dhammas, seeking the unborn, unageing, unailing, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled supreme surcease of bondage which is Nibbāna, attained to the unborn, unageing, unailing, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled supreme surcease of bondage which is Nibbāna.
mn26:30.2: ‘The knowledge and vision arose in them:
mn26:30.3: “My deliverance is unassailable. This is my last birth. There is now no renewal of being.” ‘ “
mn26:31.1: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual desire.
mn26:31.3: Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished-for, desired, agreeable and likeable, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.
mn26:31.7: Tangibles cognizable by the body … provocative of lust.
mn26:31.8: These are the five cords of sensual desire.
mn26:32.1: ‘When any monks and divines are entangled with and unwarily committed to these five cords of sensual desire and cultivate them with no vision of the danger in them and no understanding of the escape from them, it may be understood of them thus:
mn26:32.2: “They are bound for disaster, bound for ruin, to be done with as he likes by the Evil One.”
mn26:32.3: ‘Suppose a forest deer were tied to, and lay down on, a mass of snares,
mn26:32.4: it might be understood of him thus:
mn26:32.5: “He is bound for disaster, bound for ruin, to be done with as he likes by the hunter”,
mn26:32.7: so too when any monks and divines …
mn26:32.8: “… to be done with as he likes by the Evil One.”
mn26:33.1: ‘When any monks and divines are not entangled with nor unwarily committed to these five cords of sensual desire and do not cultivate them, having vision of the danger in them and understanding the escape from them, it may be understood of them thus:
mn26:33.2: “They are not bound for disaster, not bound for ruin, not to be done with as he likes by the Evil One.”
mn26:33.3: ‘Suppose a forest deer were not tied to but lay down on a mass of snares,
mn26:33.4: it might be understood of him thus.
mn26:33.5: “He is not bound for disaster, not bound for ruin, not to be done with as he likes by the hunter”,
mn26:33.7: so too when any monks and divines …
mn26:33.8: “… not to be done with as he likes by the Evil One.”’
mn26:34.1: ‘Suppose a forest deer is wandering in the forest wilds, he walks without fear, stands without fear, sits without fear, lies down without fear.
mn26:34.3: Because he is out of the hunter’s sight—
mn26:34.4: so too, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and bliss born of seclusion.
mn26:34.5: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra, to have become invisible to the Evil One by depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:35.1: ‘Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application … second jhāna … born of concentration.
mn26:35.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra, to have become invisible to the Evil One by depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:36.1: ‘Again, with the fading as well of happiness … third jhāna … “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”
mn26:36.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra … depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:37.1: ‘Again, with the abandoning of (bodily) pleasure and pain … fourth jhāna … and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn26:37.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra … depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:38.1: ‘Again, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of the perceptions of resistance, with not giving attention to perceptions of difference, (aware that) “space is infinite”, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of the infinity of space.
mn26:38.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra … depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:39.1: ‘Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of the infinity of space, (aware that) “consciousness is infinite”, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of the infinity of consciousness.
mn26:39.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra … depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:40.1: ‘Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of the infinity of consciousness, (aware that) “there is nothing”, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of nothingness.
mn26:40.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra … depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:41.1: ‘Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of nothingness a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn26:41.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra … depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity.
mn26:42.1: ‘Again, by completely surmounting the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling. And his taints are exhausted by his seeing with understanding.
mn26:42.2: And this bhikkhu is said to have blindfolded Māra, to have become invisible to the Evil One by depriving Māra’s eye of its opportunity,
mn26:42.3: and to have crossed beyond attachment to the world.’ ‘He walks without fear, stands without fear, sits without fear, lies down without fear.
mn26:42.5: He is out of the Evil One’s sight.’
mn26:42.6: That is what the Blessed One said.
mn26:42.7: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
